subject: Mathematics

source: School scheme of work: Pearson KS3 Maths Progress (2nd ed.) Year 9 Autumn, Unit 1 Indices and standard form and Unit 2 Expressions and formulae (ks3_maths_a_p_sow3.xlsx), in the scheme's order, building to GCSE 1MA1; INSET lesson standard.

lessons.title: Indices and the order of operations
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does −3² give a different answer from (−3)²?
objectives: Calculate with powers, including square brackets
Apply the order of operations with indices
Use a calculator correctly for powers of negative numbers
successCriteria: Evaluate expressions with one power and one other operation
Evaluate nested brackets and powers of negative numbers
Explain the difference between −3² and (−3)²
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: operator precedence in programming; Science: units like m²
lessons.smsc: Social: shared conventions make communication precise

keywords.def: the small number showing how many times to multiply a number by itself
the number being raised to a power
[ ] used outside round brackets in nested calculations
work out the value

teach.heading: Indices come before × and ÷
bullets: B, then I, then D/M, then A/S
The index belongs only to the number it touches

teach.heading: Calculator check
teach.note: Pupils try both on their calculators and report results in the chat.

independent: Extend: Insert brackets to make true: 2 + 3² × 4 = 100; 18 − 3² + 1 = 8
Stretch: Find the value of x² − 2x + 3 when x = −4, showing each step. Then find a negative value of x that gives 18.
lessons.homework: Write five calculations with powers where removing or moving brackets changes the answer; give both answers.
lessons.send: Support: BIDMAS step frame with a column per stage. Stretch: create calculations with a target value.

successCriteria: Square a simple fraction
Find roots of fractions and evaluate mixed calculations
Explain why squaring a fraction less than 1 makes it smaller

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: surprises in maths that challenge intuition

keywords.def: the top number of a fraction
the bottom number of a fraction
1 divided by the number; the fraction flipped
the inverse of a power

teach.heading: Powers of fractions
bullets: Apply the power to top and bottom
Fractions below 1 get smaller when squared
teach.note: Link to the big question: (1/2)² = 1/4, a quarter is smaller than a half.

teach.heading: Roots of fractions
bullets: Root the top and the bottom

check.why: 2³ = 8 and 5³ = 125. A multiplies by 3; C cubes only the numerator.

independent: Extend: A square has area 81/169 m². Find its perimeter.
Stretch: Find a fraction whose square is bigger than itself, one whose square is smaller, and one where they are equal. Explain the rule.
lessons.homework: Complete a table of x, x², x³ and √x for x = 1/4, 1/2, 0.9, 1, 4 and describe the patterns.
lessons.send: Support: fraction wall. Stretch: negative indices (preview).

lessons.title: Estimating calculations
lessons.bigQuestion: How do engineers check a calculation before trusting it with real lives?
objectives: Round to 1 significant figure to estimate
Estimate calculations including powers and roots
Judge whether an estimate is an over- or underestimate
successCriteria: Estimate products and quotients by rounding to 1 s.f.
Estimate calculations with roots, powers and fractions
Justify whether the estimate is too big or too small
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: order of magnitude in physics; Geography: estimating resources
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility to check work that affects other people

keywords.def: a digit that tells you about the size of a number
an approximate answer using rounded values
approximately equal to
an estimate smaller than the exact answer

teach.heading: Rounding roots
bullets: Round to a nearby square or cube
teach.note: Better to choose a perfect square than to round to 1 s.f. first: √47 rounded to √50 is no easier.

teach.heading: Over or under?
bullets: Numbers in the top rounded up: overestimate
Numbers in the bottom rounded up: underestimate
teach.note: In the model we rounded 9.87 up (over), √62 up (over), and 0.198 up in the bottom (under). The effects partly cancel.

check.why: 4³ = 64 and √100 = 10, so 64 − 10 = 54. B forgets to subtract the root; C adds it instead; D cubes the wrong way (4 × 3 + 9).

independent: Extend: Estimate (21.7 × 3.08²) ÷ √(15.8). Say if it is over or under and why.
Stretch: The Earth is about 150 million km from the Sun and light travels about 300 000 km per second. Estimate how long sunlight takes to reach us in minutes.
exit: Is your estimate of 9.8 × 3.1 over or under?
lessons.homework: Estimate then calculate five calculations from science or geography homework, recording the percentage difference.
lessons.send: Support: list of square and cube numbers. Stretch: order-of-magnitude problems.

lessons.title: Index laws for numbers

objectives: Use the laws of indices for multiplying and dividing powers
Raise a power to a power
Understand zero and negative indices for numbers

a power raised to another power, e.g. (2³)²
any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1
a⁻ⁿ means 1 ÷ aⁿ

teach.heading: Zero and negative indices

lessons.send: Support: expanded forms alongside each question. Stretch: fractional indices preview.

lessons.title: Standard form for large numbers

objectives: Write large numbers in standard form
Convert from standard form to ordinary numbers
Order numbers in standard form

Convert both ways and order a list
Spot numbers that look like standard form but are not
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: astronomy and chemistry; Geography: world population
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the vastness of creation (Surah Adh-Dhariyat 51:47, 'We are expanding it')

keywords.def: A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer
10 multiplied by itself, e.g. 10³ = 1000
a number written in full
the size of a number

starter: How many zeros in one million?

teach.heading: The form A × 10ⁿ
bullets: A is at least 1 and less than 10
n says how many places the digits move

teach.heading: Converting to standard form
bullets: Put the point after the first digit

steps: Place the point after the first non-zero digit: 8.1

teach.heading: Ordering
bullets: If the powers match, compare A

check.why: 6.2 with the point moved 7 places. A and D are not standard form; C moves only 6 places.

independent: Core: Write in standard form: (a) 600 000 (b) 38 000 (c) 1 250 000 (d) 470 million
Extend: The Sun is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km from Earth; Neptune about 4.5 × 10⁹ km from the Sun. Write both as ordinary numbers and say how many times further Neptune is.
Stretch: Write 45 × 10⁶ and 0.3 × 10⁹ correctly in standard form, and explain the rule you used.
lessons.homework: Find five huge numbers (e.g. distances in space, populations) and write each in standard form, ordered from smallest to largest.
lessons.send: Support: place-value grid to count moves. Stretch: converting non-standard forms.

lessons.title: Standard form for small numbers

Explain why a negative power means a small number

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the detail of creation down to the tiniest scale

keywords.def: 10⁻ⁿ means 1 ÷ 10ⁿ
A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10
one millionth of a metre, 10⁻⁶ m
a position after the decimal point

teach.heading: Negative powers of 10
teach.note: Link back to last lesson's index laws pattern.

teach.heading: Converting small numbers
bullets: Move the point to after the first non-zero digit
Count the moves: the power is negative

teach.note: Ask pupils to order a red blood cell (8 × 10⁻⁶ m), a virus (1 × 10⁻⁷ m) and a grain of sand (5 × 10⁻⁴ m).

check.why: Move the point 4 places to get 5.3, power −4. A uses a positive power; C is not standard form; D miscounts.

independent: Core: Write in standard form: (a) 0.07 (b) 0.000 41 (c) 0.000 006 (d) 0.12

lessons.send: Support: place-value grid showing decimals. Stretch: mixed large/small ordering.

find the value of the unknown that makes it true
the operation that undoes another
a number both denominators divide into

The perimeter P of a regular hexagon with side s

change the formula so a different variable is the subject
an operation that undoes another

model.problem: A rectangle is (x + 3) cm by (x − 1) cm. Its area is 5 cm more than x². Find x.

teach.heading: Fix the error
teach.note: Show three errors: (x + 2)² = x² + 4; 3⁴ × 3² = 9⁶; 5.2 × 10³ × 2 × 10⁴ = 10.4 × 10⁷. Pupils fix them.

check.q: Which is a correct proof step for 'show (n + 3)² − (n − 3)² = 12n'?
check.why: Expanding both squares works for all n. A only checks one case; C and D misuse brackets.
